Ortigia, early March. The restoration is almost finished. In the evening, on Concetta's terrace, Giulia opens an official letter that arrived that morning.
Matei, look. It's the Central Institute for Restoration that's writing to us. From Rome.
The Institute? And what do they want?
What they want is simple: the two of us. They're offering us permanent jobs in Rome, from September.
But it's Florence we have to go to in September. Bellini's workshop…
I know. The workshop, Bellini left it to us. But the salary in Rome is double. And the prestige…
What worries me is something else: who's going to tell Bellini?
It's you who's telling him. I told him last time, when I was expecting Viola.
And Graziella? The house, Pietro, the trattoria, the notches on the door…
That's exactly the problem. What we have in Florence can't be found in Rome. Not even with double the salary.
Then we already know the answer, don't we?
Maybe. But it was chance that brought us this far. Before we answer, let's go to Rome and see. You can't choose what you haven't seen.
All right. But the train ticket, I'm buying it. And I'm buying it with a window seat.
Stress on "STEE": pre-STEE-jo. GIO = "jo" in one syllable.
Stress on the FIRST syllable: BEE-vyo.
To stress part of a sentence (answering "who?", "where?", "when?"), put it between "è" and "che":
It's the Institute that's writing to us.
È a Firenze che vogliamo restare.
It's in Florence that we want to stay.
It's tomorrow that we leave (not today).
The verb "essere" agrees with the pronoun: "SONO io che…", "SEI tu che…", "SIAMO noi che…". NOT "È io che".
For a past action, Italian prefers a short construction: "è stato / è stata / sono stati + a + infinitive":
It was Giulia who found the child.
It was the fishermen who organised the dinner.
The participle agrees with the person: "è stato Matei", "è stata Giulia", "sono stati loro".

"Chi" takes a SINGULAR verb, even when it refers to several people: "Chi vuole venire alzi la mano", NOT "alzino".
4. Dislocation: the object at the front
In speech, Italians often move the object to the beginning of the sentence, as the topic, and repeat it with a pronoun. Romanian does exactly the same!
The coffee, I'll have it later.

Rome, we'll talk about it tomorrow.
Don't forget the pronoun: "Il caffè LO prendo", NOT "Il caffè prendo dopo". Without the pronoun, the sentence sounds wrong.

They left for Rome on a Tuesday morning, leaving Viola with Concetta and Turi, who had argued for a week about who should have her more. In the end it was Viola herself who found the compromise: it was with Turi that she slept, but it was with Concetta that she ate. The train left on time. It was Matei who had chosen it, and Matei, as a good railwayman's son, had checked the timetable three times.

The Central Institute for Restoration was enormous. White laboratories full of light, microscopes that cost more than a house, a library of ten thousand volumes and thirty restorers working in silence, each in front of their own masterpiece. It was the director who welcomed them, Dr Marini, an elegant, decisive woman who spoke incredibly fast. "What we saw in Syracuse impressed us," she said. "It's people like you that we're looking for."

They spent the day visiting the laboratories. Giulia saw a Raphael waiting to be cleaned and had to sit down for a moment. Matei talked for an hour with a chemist who was studying seventeenth-century pigments. Everything they had ever dreamed of was there: the means, the time, the most important paintings in Italy. And yet, as they left, neither of them spoke.

They had dinner in a trattoria in Trastevere, small and noisy, a bit like Graziella's. The waiter was friendly, the carbonara was perfect, but there was nobody who knew them. Nobody asking about Viola, no Pietro stealing the bread, no Signor Franco telling stories about trains. "That's what I miss," Giulia said at one point, without explaining what. Matei understood anyway.

That night, in a small hotel room near the station, Giulia phoned Ortigia. It was Turi who answered, whispering, because Viola was asleep on his chest. "She ate everything Concetta gave her," he reported, "and then she fell asleep while I was telling her about Saint Lucy. She's a little girl who knows how to listen." Giulia hung up and looked at the ceiling for a long time. It was Ortigia she was thinking about, not Rome.

The next morning, instead of going straight back to Sicily, they took a train to Florence. It was Giulia who suggested it. "We know the answer," she had said, "but it's Bellini we have to ask. He gave us everything. We can't decide without him."

Bellini had gone back to Florence for two weeks to settle the last few things before his retirement. He received them in his study, the one with the drawing of Totò hanging above the desk. He read the letter from Rome in silence, twice, then put it down on the table. "It's a magnificent offer," he said. "Anyone who turns it down is mad." Matei and Giulia looked at each other.

Then Bellini opened the drawer, the one where he kept his grandfather's photograph, and took out another letter, old and yellowed. It had the same letterhead stamp: Central Institute for Restoration, Rome. The date was 1995. "They offered it to me too," he said quietly. "I was thirty. It was every restorer's dream. And I said no."

"And have you never regretted it?" asked Matei. Bellini gave the faintest smile. "Sometimes, yes. Every so often, when I read in the papers about a great restoration done in Rome, I'd think: that could have been me. But then I'd come back here, open the window, hear Graziella shouting at the baker, and the regret would pass. What matters isn't where you work. It's who you find in the evening when you come home."

"Why?" asked Giulia. Bellini looked out of the window, towards the rooftops of the Oltrarno. "Because it was here that my grandfather told me 'look, and don't touch anything'. It was here that my roots were. What you learn in a place like this, you don't learn in any institute. And whoever leaves their roots, sooner or later, dries up like a plant without water."

He paused. "But that's not what you have to do. You don't have to choose what I chose. You have to choose what's right for the three of you. If you choose Rome, I'll be the first to celebrate. If you choose Florence…" He stopped, and for a moment he couldn't go on. "If you choose Florence, it will be my grandfather's workshop that celebrates."

That night they slept in their flat above the trattoria, which had been empty for six months. Graziella had left clean sheets and a bunch of flowers on the table. In the nursery, on the door frame, were Marco's notches and Viola's little one, "still in the tummy". Giulia touched it with one finger. "It's here she has to grow up," she said. "It's on this door I want to make her notches. Not on a door in Rome."

The next morning Giulia wrote the reply to Dr Marini, sitting at the kitchen table while Graziella, downstairs, made coffee for the first customers. The letter was courteous, grateful and very short. Matei wrote the last sentence: "We thank you with all our hearts, but it's in Florence that we have put down roots. And roots, as a great master taught us, cannot be moved."

When they went down to the trattoria, Graziella understood everything before they even spoke. She put down the coffee pot, wiped her hands on her apron and hugged them both at once. "I knew it," she said. "I haven't slept since you left. Now at last I can sleep." Then, laughing and crying, she added: "Viola's room, anyway, I hadn't touched it. Good things come to those who wait."

We thank you with all our hearts for your offer and for the kindness with which you received us in Rome.
It was a difficult decision. What we saw at the Institute is every restorer's dream.
However, it is in Florence that we have our family, our home and a workshop that has been entrusted to us.
We hope to be able to collaborate with the Institute in future. With our warmest regards, Matei Popa and Giulia Esposito.
